Threadfin shad (Dorosoma petenense) from marine populations along the Gulf Coast reach a maximum standard length of 19.5 centimeters [Li = 19.5 centimeters], a value derived from sampling adult fish in saltwater embayments. This ultimate size appears somewhat larger than that reported for most freshwater-resident conspecifics, suggesting that saline conditions may promote more extended somatic growth in this pelagic clupeid. During a comprehensive survey of spawning adults in Mobile Bay, gravid individuals measuring between 16 and 19 centimeters in standard length were routinely captured, confirming that asymptotic body size is attained only after several growing seasons in the coastal environment. The length-weight relationship for these marine specimens indicates that a fish of ultimate length typically achieves a corresponding wet weight of approximately 115 grams [Wwi = approximately 115 grams], a mass that reflects the energetic demands of occupying a high-salinity habitat with abundant zooplankton prey. This maximum adult mass supports robust gonad development and repeated spawning events over the course of the reproductive life span.

Assessment of gonadal development in field-collected Threadfin shad reveals that sexual maturation begins when individuals reach a standard length of 4.8 centimeters [Lp = 4.8 centimeters]. This threshold length marks the initiation of vitellogenesis in females and the onset of spermiation in males, corresponding to the period shortly after the first growing season in subtropical populations. The small size at puberty, relative to the ultimate length of 19.5 centimeters, indicates a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive activity, a common pattern among short-lived, iteroparous clupeids. In Lake Mead, for instance, young-of-year fish attaining 4.8 centimeters during their first autumn were observed to possess developing gonads by the following spring, confirming that the length-based maturation schedule is consistent across distinct geographic regions. This relatively modest body size at the onset of gonadal recrudescence allows Threadfin shad to contribute to the spawning stock within their first year, thereby maintaining high population turnover rates in both reservoir and coastal ecosystems.

The egg diameter of Threadfin shad is approximately 0.8 millimeters, and from this dimension the wet weight at birth is calculated at 0.00027 grams [Wwb = 0.00027 grams], assuming spherical egg geometry and a density equivalent to that of freshwater. These small, pelagic eggs are released during surface spawning events, where they undergo fertilization and embryonic development within the water column. The minute mass of the fertilized ovum reflects the minimal maternal investment per offspring characteristic of broadcast-spawning clupeids, a strategy that trades high fecundity for low per-capita provisioning. Following a brief incubation period, yolk-sac larvae emerge at a size that requires immediate transition to exogenous feeding, as the endogenous yolk reserves are rapidly depleted. This lecithotrophic phase is brief, and the timing of first feeding is critical for larval survival, with mortality often exceeding ninety percent during the first week due to starvation and predation on these extremely small, newly hatched individuals.

Longevity data for Threadfin shad indicate that maximum life span is approximately 1,825 days [am = approximately 1,825 days] under the thermal regime typical of temperate reservoirs, specifically at a mean annual water temperature of 20 °C [T = 20 °C]. This lifespan, equivalent to roughly five years, represents the upper limit of persistence for individuals that avoid predation and disease, with most of the population experiencing mortality well before this age. The relationship between temperature and aging is pronounced in this species: metabolic rates are elevated at warmer conditions, potentially accelerating senescence, whereas cooler waters may extend the duration of somatic maintenance but also delay reproductive maturation. Field studies in Alabama and Texas have confirmed that very few Threadfin shad exceed four years of age, with the oldest individuals typically collected from deep, thermally stratified refugia where summer temperatures remain below the lethal maximum. This relatively compressed life cycle, coupled with early maturation, defines the species as an archetypal short-lived forage fish.

Fecundity in Threadfin shad is substantial, with each female producing between approximately 2,000 and 24,000 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 2,000 and 24,000 eggs per spawning event], depending on body size and nutritional condition. Larger, older females contribute disproportionately to the egg bank, as fecundity scales positively with standard length and body mass. Spawning occurs multiple times across the reproductive season, with individual females releasing clutches at intervals of roughly 5 to 10 days; the overall frequency of reproductive events is estimated at one spawning event per week [F_R_i = one spawning event per week] during peak activity from late spring through early autumn in most of their range. This iteroparous, batch-spawning strategy ensures that the population can rapidly exploit favorable conditions for larval survival, such as phytoplankton blooms that sustain the zooplankton prey base. The combination of high fecundity per event and frequent spawning yields a substantial annual reproductive output, underpinning the species' role as a critical trophic link between plankton and piscivorous predators in reservoir food webs.
